On Complexity of Gaussian Sampling

Huanjian Zhou ††thanks: zhou-huanjian185@g.ecc.u-tokyo.ac.jp Affiliation: The University of Tokyo    Taiji Suzuki ††thanks: taiji@mist.i.u-tokyo.ac.jp Affiliation: The University of Tokyo Affiliation: RIKEN Center for Advanced Intelligence Project
Abstract

We study the number of exact matrix-vector queries needed to sample a centered dd-dimensional Gaussian with condition number at most κ\kappa to total variation error ε\varepsilon. The best known algorithm uses O⁡(min⁡{d,κ​log⁡(dε)})O(\min\{d,\sqrt{\kappa}\log(\frac{d}{\varepsilon})\}) queries, while the known lower bounds do not grow as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0 and match this bound only for κ≤d1/5−δ\kappa\leq d^{1/5-\delta} at constant accuracy. We introduce a construction based on a hidden determinant sign and prove a lower bound of Ω⁡(min⁡{d,κ​log⁡(1+dκ​ε)})\Omega\!\left(\min\left\{d,\sqrt{\kappa}\log\left(1+\frac{d}{\sqrt{\kappa}\,\varepsilon}\right)\right\}\right) uniformly for all d≥1d\geq 1, κ≥4\kappa\geq 4, and 0<ε≤1160<\varepsilon\leq\tfrac{1}{16}. This bound matches the known upper bound up to constant factors whenever κ≤d2−δ\kappa\leq d^{2-\delta} for fixed δ∈(0,2)\delta\in(0,2), or ε≤d−c\varepsilon\leq d^{-c} for fixed c>0c>0. We also extend a recent fixed-spectrum construction with a hidden eigenbasis from κ=2\kappa=2 to 2≤κ≤d1−δ2\leq\kappa\leq d^{1-\delta}, for any fixed δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1). This gives an Ωδ​(κ​log⁡d)\Omega_{\delta}(\sqrt{\kappa}\log d) lower bound at constant accuracy that holds even when the spectrum of the precision matrix is known to the algorithm.

1 Introduction

We study the problem of sampling from a centered Gaussian distribution given query access to its unnormalized density. Gaussian sampling is a fundamental algorithmic task with applications in Bayesian inference [7], numerical simulation [11], and randomized approximation algorithms [16].

The target is πA=N⁡(0,A−1)\pi_{A}=N(0,A^{-1}), where the unknown precision matrix AA satisfies Id⪯A⪯κ​IdI_{d}\preceq A\preceq\kappa I_{d}. An algorithm accesses AA through matrix–vector product queries. At each step, it chooses a vector x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and observes A​xAx. The goal of the algorithm is to output a random vector whose distribution is within ε\varepsilon of πA\pi_{A} in total variation (TV) distance. We ask how many queries required for sampling from dd-dimensional Gaussian distribution to accuracy ε\varepsilon with the condition number κ\kappa.

Gaussian sampling has a long history, with methods based on polynomial approximations to matrix square roots and inverse square roots [13, 12], Krylov subspaces and conjugate gradients [23, 4, 11], and Markov chain Monte Carlo, including Gibbs sampling and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo [25, 14, 2]. In the first-order oracle model considered here, [17] obtained a query bound of O⁡(κ​d​log3⁡(κ​dε))O(\kappa d\log^{3}(\tfrac{\kappa d}{\varepsilon})) for Metropolized Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. For Gaussian targets, [2] improved this to O~​(κ​d1/4​log⁡(1ε))\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{\kappa}\,d^{1/4}\log(\tfrac{1}{\varepsilon})) using long, randomized integration times, with initialization included in the query count. Analyses of Hit-and-Run also yield an O⁡(κ​d​log⁡(κ​dε))O(\kappa d\log(\tfrac{\kappa d}{\varepsilon})) query bound, since each exact Gaussian line update requires only one matrix-vector query [3, 8]. A sharper worst-case upper bound is provided by the polynomial sampler of [10], which requires O⁡(min⁡{d,κ​log⁡(dε)})O(\min\{d,\sqrt{\kappa}\log(\tfrac{d}{\varepsilon})\}) queries for total variation error ε\varepsilon. At a sufficiently small constant total variation error, they proved a lower bound of Ω⁡(min⁡{d,κ})\Omega(\min\{d,\sqrt{\kappa}\}) against arbitrary randomized adaptive algorithms. They further obtained Ωδ​(κ​log⁡d)\Omega_{\delta}(\sqrt{\kappa}\log d) when κ≤d1/5−δ\kappa\leq d^{1/5-\delta}, for any fixed δ∈(0,1/5)\delta\in(0,1/5), matching their upper bound at constant accuracy in this regime. They conjectured that Ω⁡(κ​log⁡d)\Omega(\sqrt{\kappa}\log d) queries are necessary whenever κ​log⁡d≤d\sqrt{\kappa}\log d\leq d. A recent preprint [22] gives an Ω⁡(log⁡d)\Omega(\log d) lower bound for κ=2\kappa=2 and ε=110\varepsilon=\frac{1}{10}, using instances with a fixed spectrum and a random eigenbasis. None of these lower bounds grows as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0, and for κ≥d1/5\kappa\geq d^{1/5} they are below the upper bound by a factor of order log⁡(d/ε)\log(d/\varepsilon).

However, both regimes arise in applications. Large condition numbers arise naturally in spatial statistics and Gaussian process regression [1, 6, 18]. On a bounded domain, the covariance matrices of a fixed Matérn model satisfy κ=Ω⁡(d)\kappa=\Omega(d) as the number dd of sampling locations increases [26]. Sparse precision matrices arising from SPDE-based Gaussian Markov random field approximations of Mat’ern fields can likewise become ill-conditioned under mesh refinement [19, 24]. For example, a regular-grid discretization of the Matérn SPDE with ν=1\nu=1 on a fixed two-dimensional periodic domain satisfies κ=Θ⁡(d2)\kappa=\Theta(d^{2}) under uniform refinement.

High sampling accuracy matters for estimating a rare failure probability pp [20], since TV error ε\varepsilon allows relative bias up to ε/p\varepsilon/p. High accuracy matters in Gibbs samplers with Gaussian conditionals [7, 21], where uncorrected sampling errors can bias the chain [15]. From a common initial law, a uniform per-update TV error of ε\varepsilon accumulates to at most N​εN\varepsilon over NN updates. In neither regime do the known bounds determine the query complexity. This leads to the following question.

Can we establish sharp lower bounds for high-accuracy sampling from ill-conditioned Gaussians, uniformly over all dimensions?

1.1 Our results

Our first result is the following lower bound, which holds for every κ≥4\kappa\geq 4 and increases as ε\varepsilon decreases to zero.

Theorem 1.1 (Informal; see Theorem 3.1).

For every integer d≥1d\geq 1, κ≥4\kappa\geq 4, and 0<ε≤1/160<\varepsilon\leq 1/16, any Gaussian sampler requires Ω⁡(min⁡{d,κ​log⁡(1+dκ​ε)})\Omega\big(\min\big\{d,\,\sqrt{\kappa}\log\big(1+\frac{d}{\sqrt{\kappa}\,\varepsilon}\big)\big\}\big) queries.

Our lower bound matches the known upper bound of O⁡(min⁡{d,κ​log⁡(dε)})O\!\big(\min\big\{d,\sqrt{\kappa}\log(\tfrac{d}{\varepsilon})\big\}\big) up to constant factors whenever κ≤d2−δ\kappa\leq d^{2-\delta} for any fixed δ∈(0,2)\delta\in(0,2). At constant accuracy, the two bounds were previously known to match only for κ≤d1/5−δ\kappa\leq d^{1/5-\delta}. This confirms the conjecture of [10] that Ω⁡(κ​log⁡d)\Omega(\sqrt{\kappa}\log d) queries are necessary at constant accuracy whenever κ​log⁡d≤d\sqrt{\kappa}\log d\leq d. It also matches the upper bound for every κ≥4\kappa\geq 4 whenever ε≤d−c\varepsilon\leq d^{-c} for any fixed c>0c>0. For κ≥d2\kappa\geq d^{2}, it yields the optimal Θ⁡(d)\Theta(d) query complexity.

We also extend the hidden-eigenbasis construction of [22] to obtain an Ωδ​(κ​log⁡d)\Omega_{\delta}(\sqrt{\kappa}\log d) lower bound for 2≤κ≤d1−δ2\leq\kappa\leq d^{1-\delta}. We summarize the comparisons in Table 1.

Theorem 1.2 (Informal; see Theorem 4.1).

For every fixed δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), sufficiently large dd, 2≤κ≤d1−δ2\leq\kappa\leq d^{1-\delta}, and 0<ε≤1/100<\varepsilon\leq 1/10, any Gaussian sampler requires Ωδ​(κ​log⁡d)\Omega_{\delta}(\sqrt{\kappa}\log d) queries.

This bound is tight at constant accuracy and, more generally, whenever d−C≤ε≤1/10d^{-C}\leq\varepsilon\leq 1/10 for a fixed C>0C>0, with matching constants depending on δ\delta and CC. For κ≥4\kappa\geq 4 and ε≤116\varepsilon\leq\frac{1}{16} it is implied by Theorem 3.1 while the new cases are 2≤κ<42\leq\kappa<4 and 116<ε≤110\frac{1}{16}<\varepsilon\leq\frac{1}{10}. We include it because its hard instances have a fixed spectrum, so the bound holds even for algorithms that know the spectrum of the precision matrix. Section 4.4 explains why the analysis of these instances gives no dependence on ε\varepsilon and does not extend beyond κ=d1−δ\kappa=d^{1-\delta}.

Remark 1.3 (Connection to strongly log-concave sampling).

Our lower bounds also apply to sampling from π∝e−V\pi\propto e^{-V} with Id⪯∇2V⪯κ​IdI_{d}\preceq\nabla^{2}V\preceq\kappa I_{d} using exact value-and-gradient queries, even when the minimizer is known. For κ=2\kappa=2 and TV accuracy 1/101/10, [22] establishes an Oη​(dη)O_{\eta}(d^{\eta}) upper bound for every fixed η>0\eta>0, leaving a gap from the Ω⁡(log⁡d)\Omega(\log d) lower bound, whereas Gaussian sampling has complexity Θ⁡(log⁡d)\Theta(\log d) in this regime. For general condition numbers and high accuracy, [9] obtain TV error ε\varepsilon using O~​(κ​d1/4​polylog⁡(1/ε))\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{\kappa}\,d^{1/4}\operatorname{polylog}(1/\varepsilon)) expected gradient queries with a warm start. Thus, our results provide an improved lower bounds for general strongly log-concave sampling with almost tight lower bounds for Gaussian subclass.

2 Preliminaries

We write ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| for the Euclidean norm and IdI_{d} for the d×dd\times d identity matrix. For symmetric matrices AA and BB, the notation A⪯BA\preceq B means that B−AB-A is positive semidefinite.

Let O⁡(n):={O∈ℝn×n:O⊤​O=In}O(n):=\{O\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}:O^{\top}O=I_{n}\} denote the real orthogonal group, equipped with Haar probability measure. It has two components, {detO=+1}\{\det O=+1\}, {detO=−1}\{\det O=-1\}, and each have Haar probability 1/21/2. For b∈{−1,+1}b\in\{-1,+1\}, we write μn,b\mu_{n,b} for Haar probability measure conditioned on detO=b\det O=b.

Targets and oracle.

We restrict the target class to centered Gaussians. This restriction removes the hardness of locating the target and isolates the difficulty of sampling with an unknown covariance. For an integer d≥1d\geq 1 and a parameter κ≥1\kappa\geq 1, without loss of generality, we normalize the spectral bounds to 11 and κ\kappa by rescaling and consider the precision class

𝒜d,κ:={A∈ℝd×d:A=A⊤,Id⪯A⪯κId}.\mathcal{A}_{d,\kappa}:=\left\{A\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}:A=A^{\top},\quad I_{d}\preceq A\preceq\kappa I_{d}\right\}.

An input A∈𝒜d,κA\in\mathcal{A}_{d,\kappa} specifies the quadratic potential fA​(x):=12​x⊤​A​xf_{A}(x):=\frac{1}{2}x^{\top}Ax and the target distribution πA:=N⁡(0,A−1)\pi_{A}:=N(0,A^{-1}). At a point x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, the exact first-order oracle returns

FOA⁡(x):=(fA​(x),∇fA​(x))=(12​x⊤​A​x,A​x).\operatorname{FO}_{A}(x):=\bigl(f_{A}(x),\nabla f_{A}(x)\bigr)=\left(\frac{1}{2}x^{\top}Ax,Ax\right). (1)

On this class, exact first-order access is equivalent to exact matrix–vector access. Indeed, a first-order response contains A​xAx, while a matrix–vector response determines both the gradient A​xAx and the function value 12​⟨x,A​x⟩\frac{1}{2}\langle x,Ax\rangle. Thus the exact value-and-gradient, gradient-only, and matrix–vector query complexities coincide.

Randomized algorithms.

A randomized algorithm chooses its queries and stopping decisions as Borel functions of its internal randomness and previous oracle responses, where the randomness is independent of the input. Its output may be any ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}-valued Borel function of the same information. The algorithm has fixed query budget TT if it makes at most TT queries for every admissible input and every realization of its internal randomness.

Accuracy measures.

For probability measures PP and QQ on a common measurable space, their total variation distance is

TV⁡(P,Q):=supB|P⁡(B)−Q⁡(B)|=12​∫|p−q|​𝑑λ,\operatorname{TV}(P,Q):=\sup_{B}|P(B)-Q(B)|=\frac{1}{2}\int|p-q|\,d\lambda,

where the supremum ranges over measurable sets, and pp and qq are the densities of PP and QQ with respect to any common dominating measure λ\lambda. In particular, |𝔼P​h−𝔼Q​h|≤TV⁡(P,Q)|\mathbb{E}_{P}h-\mathbb{E}_{Q}h|\leq\operatorname{TV}(P,Q) for every measurable function hh taking values in [0,1][0,1].

Sampling accuracy and query complexity.

For a fixed input AA, let ρAAlg\rho_{A}^{\mathrm{Alg}} denote the law of the algorithm’s output, with all internal randomness included. For 0<ε<10<\varepsilon<1, define

QG​(d,κ,ε):=inf{T∈ℤ≥0:∃Alg​ with fixed query budget ​Tsuch that ​supA∈𝒜d,κTV⁡(ρAAlg,πA)≤ε}.Q_{G}(d,\kappa,\varepsilon):=\inf\left\{T\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}:\begin{array}[]{l}\exists\,\mathrm{Alg}\text{ with fixed query budget }T\\[2.0pt] \text{such that }\displaystyle\sup_{A\in\mathcal{A}_{d,\kappa}}\operatorname{TV}\bigl(\rho_{A}^{\mathrm{Alg}},\pi_{A}\bigr)\leq\varepsilon\end{array}\right\}. (2)

The accuracy requirement is uniform over inputs and concerns the output law after averaging over the algorithm’s seed. Throughout the paper, query budgets are deterministic caps on the number of queries in each run, rather than bounds on the expected number of queries.

3 Lower Bound via Hidden Determinant Sign

In this section, we establish a Gaussian sampling lower bound that holds uniformly for all dimensions d≥1d\geq 1, arbitrarily large condition-number bounds κ≥4\kappa\geq 4, and arbitrarily small total variation errors 0<ε≤1/160<\varepsilon\leq 1/16.

Theorem 3.1 (Gaussian sampling lower bound).

For every integer d≥1d\geq 1, κ≥4\kappa\geq 4, and 0<ε≤1/160<\varepsilon\leq 1/16,

QG​(d,κ,ε)≥1256​min⁡{d,κ​log⁡(1+dκ​ε)}.Q_{G}(d,\kappa,\varepsilon)\geq\frac{1}{256}\min\left\{d,\,\sqrt{\kappa}\log\left(1+\frac{d}{\sqrt{\kappa}\,\varepsilon}\right)\right\}. (3)

In the remainder of this section, we present the construction in Section 3.1, state its three key properties in Section 3.2, and use them to prove Theorem 3.1 in Section 3.3. The proofs of these properties are deferred to Sections B.1, B.2 and B.3.

3.1 The Hard Gaussian Family

Fix κ≥4\kappa\geq 4. Let 3≤n≤d3\leq n\leq d be the block dimension and k:=⌊d/n⌋k:=\lfloor d/n\rfloor the number of blocks. In the proof of the main theorem, we choose n=2​T+1n=2T+1, where TT is the algorithm’s query budget. This choice applies when T≥1T\geq 1 and 2​T+1≤d2T+1\leq d. The remaining cases are treated separately. For O∈O⁡(n)O\in O(n), define

AO:=κ+12​In−κ−14​(O+O⊤).A_{O}:=\frac{\kappa+1}{2}I_{n}-\frac{\kappa-1}{4}(O+O^{\top}). (4)

For 𝑶=(O1,…,Ok)∈O​(n)k\bm{O}=(O_{1},\ldots,O_{k})\in O(n)^{k}, set

A𝑶:=diag⁡(AO1,…,AOk,Id−k​n).A_{\bm{O}}:=\operatorname{diag}\bigl(A_{O_{1}},\ldots,A_{O_{k}},I_{d-kn}\bigr). (5)

For each b∈{−1,+1}b\in\{-1,+1\}, draw O1,…,OkO_{1},\ldots,O_{k} independently from μn,b\mu_{n,b}, and let 𝒟b\mathcal{D}_{b} denote the law of A𝑶A_{\bm{O}}. Thus the orthogonal matrices share the same determinant sign.

Writing Pb:=𝔼O∼μn,b​[N⁡(0,AO−1)]P_{b}:=\mathbb{E}_{O\sim\mu_{n,b}}[N(0,A_{O}^{-1})] for the single-block target mixture, the averaged target under 𝒟b\mathcal{D}_{b} is

π¯b:=𝔼A∼𝒟b​[πA]=Pb⊗k⊗N⁡(0,Id−k​n).\bar{\pi}_{b}:=\mathbb{E}_{A\sim\mathcal{D}_{b}}[\pi_{A}]=P_{b}^{\otimes k}\otimes N(0,I_{d-kn}). (6)

When k​n=dkn=d, the identity block and the final Gaussian factor are omitted.

3.2 Properties of the Construction

This subsection states the three lemmas used in the proof of Theorem 3.1. Lemma 3.2 shows that an algorithm with fewer than n/2n/2 queries has the same average output law under the two priors, Lemma 3.3 shows that the two averaged targets are far apart in total variation, and Lemma 3.4 verifies that the hard family belongs to 𝒜d,κ\mathcal{A}_{d,\kappa}. All proofs are deferred to Appendix B.

Why the priors are indistinguishable.

A first-order query can be simulated by observing O​vOv and O⊤​vO^{\top}v in each block and each of these two observations fixes at most one new direction of the unknown orthogonal map. Conditionally on the history, the rest of OjO_{j} is Haar distributed subject to its determinant sign, and as long as two dimensions are unexplored the next response has the same law under either sign. The condition 2​T<n2T<n ensures this at every observation, including when queries depend on responses from other blocks. The proof is in Section B.1.

Lemma 3.2 (Indistinguishability).

For every randomized first-order algorithm Alg\mathrm{Alg} with query budget T<n/2T<n/2,

𝔼A∼𝒟+1​[ρAAlg]=𝔼A∼𝒟−1​[ρAAlg].\mathbb{E}_{A\sim\mathcal{D}_{+1}}[\rho_{A}^{\mathrm{Alg}}]=\mathbb{E}_{A\sim\mathcal{D}_{-1}}[\rho_{A}^{\mathrm{Alg}}]. (7)
Why the target mixtures remain separated.

Although low query budget algorithm cannot detect the determinant sign, the norm of a target sample carries information about it. Comparing the expectations of the radial test function x↦e−λ​‖x‖2x\mapsto e^{-\lambda\|x\|^{2}} under the two single-block mixtures gives TV(P+1,P−1)≥12e−5n/κ\mathrm{TV}(P_{+1},P_{-1})\geq\frac{1}{2}e^{-5n/\sqrt{\kappa}}. A sample from the full target consists of kk blocks that are independent given the common sign, and tensorization of the Hellinger affinity amplifies the single-block separation to the bound below. Adding blocks does not help the algorithm, since a single query already acts on all blocks and Lemma 3.2 holds for every kk. We summarize this property in Lemma 3.3, whose proof is given in Section B.2.

Lemma 3.3 (Separation).

The averaged targets satisfy

TV⁡(π¯+1,π¯−1)≥1−exp⁡{−k8​exp⁡(−10​nκ)}.\operatorname{TV}(\bar{\pi}_{+1},\bar{\pi}_{-1})\geq 1-\exp\left\{-\frac{k}{8}\exp\left(-\frac{10n}{\sqrt{\kappa}}\right)\right\}. (8)
Why the construction satisfies the regularity assumptions.

The symmetric part (O+O⊤)/2(O+O^{\top})/2 has spectrum in [−1,1][-1,1]. The affine transformation in Eq. (4) therefore places the spectrum of AOA_{O} in [1,κ][1,\kappa]. Forming a block-diagonal matrix and adding an identity block preserves these bounds. This gives the following lemma with proof in Section B.3.

Lemma 3.4 (Regularity).

For every 𝐎∈O​(n)k\bm{O}\in O(n)^{k}, A𝐎∈𝒜d,κA_{\bm{O}}\in\mathcal{A}_{d,\kappa}. The potential fA𝐎f_{A_{\bm{O}}} has unique minimizer 00 and minimum value 00.

3.3 Proof of Theorem 3.1

Let Alg\mathrm{Alg} have fixed query budget TT and satisfy TV⁡(ρAAlg,πA)≤ε\operatorname{TV}(\rho_{A}^{\mathrm{Alg}},\pi_{A})\leq\varepsilon for every A∈𝒜d,κA\in\mathcal{A}_{d,\kappa}.

Zero-query cases.

A zero-query algorithm has the same output distribution on A0=IdA_{0}=I_{d} and A1=diag⁡(κ,1,…,1)A_{1}=\operatorname{diag}(\kappa,1,\ldots,1). However, evaluating the event {|x1|≤1/2}\{|x_{1}|\leq 1/2\} and using κ≥4\kappa\geq 4 gives

TV⁡(πA0,πA1)≥2​∫1/21e−t2/22​π​𝑑t≥e−1/22​π>18≥2​ε,\operatorname{TV}(\pi_{A_{0}},\pi_{A_{1}})\geq 2\int_{1/2}^{1}\frac{e^{-t^{2}/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\,dt\geq\frac{e^{-1/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}>\frac{1}{8}\geq 2\varepsilon,

contradicting the triangle inequality. Thus T≥1T\geq 1. If 2​T+1>d2T+1>d, integrality gives T≥d/2T\geq d/2, which proves the claimed bound. Henceforth assume 2​T+1≤d2T+1\leq d.

Comparing the two priors.

Choose n:=2​T+1n:=2T+1 and k:=⌊d/n⌋k:=\lfloor d/n\rfloor. Then 3≤n≤d3\leq n\leq d and 2​T<n2T<n, so Lemma 3.2 gives a common averaged output distribution ρ¯\bar{\rho} under the two priors. By Lemma 3.4 and convexity of total variation under mixing,

TV⁡(ρ¯,π¯b)≤𝔼A∼𝒟b​[TV⁡(ρAAlg,πA)]≤ε,b∈{−1,+1}.\operatorname{TV}(\bar{\rho},\bar{\pi}_{b})\leq\mathbb{E}_{A\sim\mathcal{D}_{b}}\left[\operatorname{TV}(\rho_{A}^{\mathrm{Alg}},\pi_{A})\right]\leq\varepsilon,\qquad b\in\{-1,+1\}.

The triangle inequality and Lemma 3.3 therefore imply

1−exp{−k8e−10n/κ}≤TV(π¯+1,π¯−1)≤2ε.1-\exp\left\{-\frac{k}{8}e^{-10n/\sqrt{\kappa}}\right\}\leq\operatorname{TV}(\bar{\pi}_{+1},\bar{\pi}_{-1})\leq 2\varepsilon.

Rearranging yields

ke−10n/κ≤−8log(1−2ε)≤32ε,ke^{-10n/\sqrt{\kappa}}\leq-8\log(1-2\varepsilon)\leq 32\varepsilon, (9)

where the last inequality uses −log⁡(1−2​ε)=∫02​ε(1−t)−1​𝑑t≤4​ε-\log(1-2\varepsilon)=\int_{0}^{2\varepsilon}(1-t)^{-1}\,dt\leq 4\varepsilon.

Bounding the query budget.

Since k≥d/(2​n)k\geq d/(2n) and n=2​T+1≤3​Tn=2T+1\leq 3T, Eq. (9) gives

d64​ε≤n​e10​n/κ≤3​T​e30​T/κ.\frac{d}{64\varepsilon}\leq ne^{10n/\sqrt{\kappa}}\leq 3Te^{30T/\sqrt{\kappa}}. (10)

Using sinh⁡t≥t\sinh t\geq t for t≥0t\geq 0, we obtain

e60​T/κ−1=2​e30​T/κ​sinh⁡(30​Tκ)≥60​Tκ​e30​T/κ≥5​d16​κ​ε.e^{60T/\sqrt{\kappa}}-1=2e^{30T/\sqrt{\kappa}}\sinh\left(\frac{30T}{\sqrt{\kappa}}\right)\geq\frac{60T}{\sqrt{\kappa}}e^{30T/\sqrt{\kappa}}\geq\frac{5d}{16\sqrt{\kappa}\varepsilon}.

Taking logarithms and using concavity of the logarithm,

T≥κ60​log⁡(1+5​d16​κ​ε)≥κ192​log⁡(1+dκ​ε).T\geq\frac{\sqrt{\kappa}}{60}\log\left(1+\frac{5d}{16\sqrt{\kappa}\varepsilon}\right)\geq\frac{\sqrt{\kappa}}{192}\log\left(1+\frac{d}{\sqrt{\kappa}\varepsilon}\right).

The second inequality follows by writing 1+5​d/(16​κ​ε)=(11/16)+(5/16)​(1+d/(κ​ε))1+5d/(16\sqrt{\kappa}\varepsilon)=(11/16)+(5/16)(1+d/(\sqrt{\kappa}\varepsilon)).

Combining this with the alternative T≥d/2T\geq d/2 yields

T≥1256​min⁡{d,κ​log⁡(1+dκ​ε)}.T\geq\frac{1}{256}\min\left\{d,\,\sqrt{\kappa}\log\left(1+\frac{d}{\sqrt{\kappa}\varepsilon}\right)\right\}.

Since Alg\mathrm{Alg} was arbitrary, this proves the bound for QG​(d,κ,ε)Q_{G}(d,\kappa,\varepsilon).

4 Lower Bound via Hidden Eigenbasis

The preprint [22] proved an Ω⁡(log⁡d)\Omega(\log d) query lower bound for centered Gaussian sampling with Id⪯A⪯2​IdI_{d}\preceq A\preceq 2I_{d} at total variation accuracy ε=110\varepsilon=\frac{1}{10}. We subsequently examine the limitations of this analysis for establishing accuracy-dependent lower bounds in Section 4.4.

Theorem 4.1 (Extension to general κ\kappa).

For every fixed δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), there exists d0​(δ)d_{0}(\delta) such that, for every integer d≥d0​(δ)d\geq d_{0}(\delta), 2≤κ≤d1−δ2\leq\kappa\leq d^{1-\delta}, and 0<ε≤1/100<\varepsilon\leq 1/10,

QG​(d,κ,ε)≥δ256​κ​log⁡d.Q_{G}(d,\kappa,\varepsilon)\geq\frac{\delta}{256}\sqrt{\kappa}\log d.

Compared with Theorem 3.1, this bound also covers 2≤κ<42\leq\kappa<4 and 116<ε≤110\frac{1}{16}<\varepsilon\leq\frac{1}{10}, and it holds even when the spectrum of AA is known to the algorithm. On the other hand, it does not grow as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0 and it requires κ≤d1−δ\kappa\leq d^{1-\delta}.

4.1 The Hard Family

We use a construction similar to that in [22, Section 9.2], with a cosine eigenvalue grid (Chebyshev nodes) and a random orthogonal rotation, while extending the spectral interval from [1,2][1,2] to [1,κ][1,\kappa]. For d≥2d\geq 2 and κ≥2\kappa\geq 2, define

θi=(i−12)​πd,λi=κ+12+κ−12cosθi,Λ=diag(λ1,…,λd).\theta_{i}=\frac{(i-\tfrac{1}{2})\pi}{d},\qquad\lambda_{i}=\frac{\kappa+1}{2}+\frac{\kappa-1}{2}\cos\theta_{i},\qquad\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{d}). (11)

Draw O∼Haar⁡(O⁡(d))O\sim\operatorname{Haar}(\mathrm{O}(d)), independently of the algorithm’s private randomness, and set A=O​Λ​O⊤A=O\Lambda O^{\top}. The associated potential and target are fA​(x)=x⊤​A​x/2f_{A}(x)=x^{\top}Ax/2 and πA=N⁡(0,A−1)\pi_{A}=N(0,A^{-1}).

The spectrum is deterministic and may be supplied to the algorithm. In particular, the Gaussian normalizing constant is known. The unknown component is the random eigenbasis represented by OO.

Remark 4.2 (Comparison with κ=2\kappa=2 case).

At κ=2\kappa=2, the spectrum in Eq. (11) recovers the original construction in [22]. More generally, if A2A_{2} denotes the original precision matrix with the same rotation OO, then A=(κ−1)​A2−(κ−2)​IdA=(\kappa-1)A_{2}-(\kappa-2)I_{d}. Thus one matrix–vector reply for either matrix determines the corresponding reply for the other. The proof compares ∑icos⁡(n​θi)​⟨x,O​ei⟩2\sum_{i}\cos(n\theta_{i})\langle x,Oe_{i}\rangle^{2} with ‖x‖2\|x\|^{2}, where n=2​q+1n=2q+1. For the output of a qq-query algorithm, the ratio is at most d−Ω⁡(1)d^{-\Omega(1)} in absolute value (Lemma 4.4), whereas under the target the ratio of the means has absolute value e−Θ⁡(n/κ)e^{-\Theta(n/\sqrt{\kappa})} (Lemma 4.5). Hence the test works for nn up to order κ​log⁡d\sqrt{\kappa}\log d, rather than log⁡d\log d as at κ=2\kappa=2, which is the source of the factor κ\sqrt{\kappa} in Theorem 4.1.

4.2 Properties of the Hard Family

This subsection states the four lemmas used in the proof of Theorem 4.1. Lemma 4.3 places the output of any qq-query algorithm in a block Krylov space generated by independent Gaussian vectors, Lemma 4.4 bounds a quadratic form with cosine weights uniformly over this space, Lemma 4.5 evaluates the same quadratic form under the target, and Lemma 4.6 verifies that the hard family is admissible. All proofs are deferred to Appendix C.

Krylov representation of the output.

We first control the information revealed by adaptive queries via a standard Krylov argument. The deferred-rotation argument of [22, Lemma 9.2] uses the rotational symmetry of the undisclosed eigenbasis to represent the algorithm’s output in a block Krylov space generated by independent Gaussian vectors.

For vectors g1,…,gq+1∈ℝdg_{1},\ldots,g_{q+1}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and Λ=diag⁡(λ1,…,λd)\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{d}), define

𝒦q(g1,…,gq+1)=span{Λjga:1≤a≤q+1, 0≤j≤q}.\mathcal{K}_{q}(g_{1},\ldots,g_{q+1})=\operatorname{span}\{\Lambda^{j}g_{a}:1\leq a\leq q+1,\ 0\leq j\leq q\}.
Lemma 4.3 (Krylov representation).

Fix an integer q≥0q\geq 0 with 2​q+1<d2q+1<d and let XX be the output. There exist independent vectors g1,…,gq+1∼N⁡(0,Id)g_{1},\ldots,g_{q+1}\sim N(0,I_{d}) such that

O⊤​X∈𝒦q​(g1,…,gq+1)almost surely.O^{\top}X\in\mathcal{K}_{q}(g_{1},\ldots,g_{q+1})\qquad\text{almost surely}.

The additional starting vector accounts for the output, which may lie outside the span of the query points and oracle replies. Equivalently, the lemma gives a representation O⊤​X=∑a=1q+1pa​(Λ)​gaO^{\top}X=\sum_{a=1}^{q+1}p_{a}(\Lambda)g_{a}, where each pap_{a} has degree at most qq. The polynomial coefficients may depend on the entire extended experiment. We therefore control the output through an estimate that holds simultaneously for every vector in 𝒦q\mathcal{K}_{q}. The proof of Lemma 4.3 is deferred to Appendix C.1.

A uniform bound on the Krylov space.

We next control a high-frequency cosine statistic uniformly over the space in Lemma 4.3. For a query budget qq, set

n=2​q+1,Dn=diag⁡(cos⁡(n​θ1),…,cos⁡(n​θd)).n=2q+1,\qquad D_{n}=\operatorname{diag}\bigl(\cos(n\theta_{1}),\ldots,\cos(n\theta_{d})\bigr).

The choice of nn places this statistic above all frequencies arising from products of two degree-qq cosine polynomials.

Lemma 4.4 (Uniform bound on the Krylov space).

There is an absolute constant C>0C>0 such that the following holds. Let q≥0q\geq 0 satisfy 2​q+1<d2q+1<d, let g1,…,gq+1g_{1},\ldots,g_{q+1} be independent N⁡(0,Id)N(0,I_{d}) vectors, and let 𝒦q=𝒦q​(g1,…,gq+1)\mathcal{K}_{q}=\mathcal{K}_{q}(g_{1},\ldots,g_{q+1}). Define

τd,q=C⁡[(q+1)​log⁡dd+(q+1)​(q+1+log⁡d)​log⁡dd].\tau_{d,q}=C\left[(q+1)\sqrt{\frac{\log d}{d}}+\frac{(q+1)(q+1+\log d)\log d}{d}\right].

If τd,q≤1/2\tau_{d,q}\leq 1/2, then, with probability at least 0.990.99,

|u⊤​Dn​u|≤2​τd,q​‖u‖2for every ​u∈𝒦q.|u^{\top}D_{n}u|\leq 2\tau_{d,q}\|u\|^{2}\qquad\text{for every }u\in\mathcal{K}_{q}.

The proof is deferred to Appendix C.2. Since λi\lambda_{i} is a nonconstant affine function of cos⁡θi\cos\theta_{i}, the space 𝒦q\mathcal{K}_{q} is equivalently spanned by the vectors ((ga)i​cos⁡(j​θi))i=1d\bigl((g_{a})_{i}\cos(j\theta_{i})\bigr)_{i=1}^{d}, with a≤q+1a\leq q+1 and j≤qj\leq q. Consequently, the estimate is independent of κ\kappa.

On the event in Lemma 4.4, the output representation in Lemma 4.3 therefore gives

|X⊤​O​Dn​O⊤​X|≤2​τd,q​‖X‖2.\bigl|X^{\top}OD_{n}O^{\top}X\bigr|\leq 2\tau_{d,q}\|X\|^{2}.
Target moments.

We now evaluate the same cosine statistic under the target Gaussian.

Lemma 4.5 (Moments under the target).

Let κ≥2\kappa\geq 2, U∼N⁡(0,Λ−1)U\sim N(0,\Lambda^{-1}), and ϱκ=κ−1κ+1\varrho_{\kappa}=\tfrac{\sqrt{\kappa}-1}{\sqrt{\kappa}+1}. For an integer 1≤n<d1\leq n<d, put Dn=diag⁡(cos⁡(n​θi))D_{n}=\operatorname{diag}(\cos(n\theta_{i})), M=𝔼​‖U‖2M=\mathbb{E}\|U\|^{2}, and μn=𝔼⁡[U⊤​Dn​U]\mu_{n}=\mathbb{E}[U^{\top}D_{n}U]. Then

M\displaystyle M =dκ​1−ϱκ2​d1+ϱκ2​d,and ​(−1)n​μn=dκ​ϱκn−ϱκ2​d−n1+ϱκ2​d.\displaystyle=\frac{d}{\sqrt{\kappa}}\frac{1-\varrho_{\kappa}^{2d}}{1+\varrho_{\kappa}^{2d}},\quad\mbox{and }(-1)^{n}\mu_{n}=\frac{d}{\sqrt{\kappa}}\frac{\varrho_{\kappa}^{n}-\varrho_{\kappa}^{2d-n}}{1+\varrho_{\kappa}^{2d}}.

Moreover, both Var⁡(‖U‖2)\operatorname{Var}(\|U\|^{2}) and Var⁡(U⊤​Dn​U)\operatorname{Var}(U^{\top}D_{n}U) are at most 2​M≤2​d/κ2M\leq 2d/\sqrt{\kappa}.

If d−n≥κd-n\geq\sqrt{\kappa}, then

(1−e−4)e−3n/κ≤|μn|M≤e−2n/κ.(1-e^{-4})e^{-3n/\sqrt{\kappa}}\leq\frac{|\mu_{n}|}{M}\leq e^{-2n/\sqrt{\kappa}}.

The proof is deferred to Appendix C.3. For an exact sample Y|O∼πAY\mid O\sim\pi_{A}, the vector U=O⊤​YU=O^{\top}Y has law N⁡(0,Λ−1)N(0,\Lambda^{-1}), with ‖Y‖2=‖U‖2\|Y\|^{2}=\|U\|^{2} and Y⊤​O​Dn​O⊤​Y=U⊤​Dn​UY^{\top}OD_{n}O^{\top}Y=U^{\top}D_{n}U. The lemma therefore gives the means and variances of ‖Y‖2\|Y\|^{2} and Y⊤​O​Dn​O⊤​YY^{\top}OD_{n}O^{\top}Y under the target.

Admissibility and oracle equivalence.

We finally verify that the hard family belongs to the prescribed class. The proof is deferred to Appendix C.4.

Lemma 4.6 (Admissibility).

For every O∈O⁡(d)O\in\mathrm{O}(d), the matrix A=O​Λ​O⊤A=O\Lambda O^{\top} satisfies Id⪯A⪯κ​IdI_{d}\preceq A\preceq\kappa I_{d}.

4.3 Proof of Theorem 4.1

We compare the probabilities of a single test event under algorithmic outputs and target samples.

Proof of Theorem 4.1.

Fix δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), 2≤κ≤d1−δ2\leq\kappa\leq d^{1-\delta}, and 0<ε≤1/100<\varepsilon\leq 1/10. Suppose that an algorithm uses at most q≤(δ/256)​κ​log⁡dq\leq(\delta/256)\sqrt{\kappa}\log d queries and satisfies TV⁡(ρAAlg,πA)≤ε\operatorname{TV}(\rho_{A}^{\mathrm{Alg}},\pi_{A})\leq\varepsilon for every admissible AA. Lemma 4.6 makes the hard family admissible.

Set n=2​q+1n=2q+1 and τ=τd,q\tau=\tau_{d,q}. Define statistic SAS_{A} and the associated test event EAE_{A} as

SA​(x)\displaystyle S_{A}(x) :=(−1)n​x⊤​Tn​(2​A−(κ+1)​Idκ−1)​x−2​τ​‖x‖2,\displaystyle:=(-1)^{n}x^{\top}T_{n}\!\left(\frac{2A-(\kappa+1)I_{d}}{\kappa-1}\right)x-2\tau\|x\|^{2},
EA\displaystyle E_{A} :={x:SA​(x)>0},\displaystyle:=\{x:S_{A}(x)>0\},

where TnT_{n} is the degree-nn Chebyshev polynomial of the first kind.

Geometrically, for x≠0x\neq 0, the weights wi​(x)=|⟨x,O​ei⟩|2/‖x‖2w_{i}(x)=|\langle x,Oe_{i}\rangle|^{2}/\|x\|^{2} describe the fractions of its energy ‖x‖2\|x\|^{2} carried by the eigenvectors O​eiOe_{i} of AA. Using Tn​(cos⁡θi)=cos⁡(n​θi)T_{n}(\cos\theta_{i})=\cos(n\theta_{i}), the event x∈EAx\in E_{A} is equivalent to (−1)n​∑iwi​(x)​cos⁡(n​θi)>2​τ(-1)^{n}\sum_{i}w_{i}(x)\cos(n\theta_{i})>2\tau. So EAE_{A} is the event that the cosine coefficient ∑iwi​(x)​cos⁡(n​θi)\sum_{i}w_{i}(x)\cos(n\theta_{i}) of these weights at frequency nn exceeds 2​τ2\tau in absolute value and has the sign that it has under the target.

Algorithmic outputs rarely pass the test.

The bound on qq gives q+1≤d(1−δ)/2​log⁡dq+1\leq d^{(1-\delta)/2}\log d, so n=o⁡(d)n=o(d). Substituting this bound into the definition of τ\tau yields

τ≲d−δ/2(logd)3/2+d−δ(logd)3≲d−δ/2(logd)3⟶0\tau\lesssim d^{-\delta/2}(\log d)^{3/2}+d^{-\delta}(\log d)^{3}\lesssim d^{-\delta/2}(\log d)^{3}\longrightarrow 0

Thus n<dn<d and τ≤1/2\tau\leq 1/2 for sufficiently large dd depending only on δ\delta, and the Lemma 4.3 and Lemma 4.4 apply. Let XX be the algorithmic output on the random input A=O​Λ​O⊤A=O\Lambda O^{\top}. Lemma 4.3 places O⊤​XO^{\top}X in 𝒦q\mathcal{K}_{q} on an extension preserving the joint law of (O,X)(O,X). Lemma 4.4 then gives

|X⊤​O​Dn​O⊤​X|≤2​τ​‖X‖2|X^{\top}OD_{n}O^{\top}X|\leq 2\tau\|X\|^{2}

with probability at least 0.990.99. On this event, SA​(X)≤0S_{A}(X)\leq 0. Consequently,

𝔼A​[ρAAlg​(EA)]≤0.01.\mathbb{E}_{A}[\rho_{A}^{\mathrm{Alg}}(E_{A})]\leq 0.01.
Target samples typically pass the test.

Let M=tr⁡(Λ−1)M=\operatorname{tr}(\Lambda^{-1}) denote the target mean squared norm, and let μn=tr⁡(Dn​Λ−1)\mu_{n}=\operatorname{tr}(D_{n}\Lambda^{-1}) denote the target mean of the cosine statistic. Write β=|μn|/M\beta=|\mu_{n}|/M for the normalized target bias.

Since n=o⁡(d)n=o(d) and κ≤d(1−δ)/2=o⁡(d)\sqrt{\kappa}\leq d^{(1-\delta)/2}=o(d), we have d−n≥κd-n\geq\sqrt{\kappa} for sufficiently large dd. Lemma 4.5 and the the bound on qq therefore give

β≥(1−e−4)e−3n/κ≥bd−δ/4,b=(1−e−4)e−3,\beta\geq(1-e^{-4})e^{-3n/\sqrt{\kappa}}\geq b\,d^{-\delta/4},\qquad b=(1-e^{-4})e^{-3},

where we used 3​n/κ≤3+(3​δ/128)​log⁡d3n/\sqrt{\kappa}\leq 3+(3\delta/128)\log d. Moreover, ϱκ≤e−1/κ\varrho_{\kappa}\leq e^{-1/\sqrt{\kappa}} and d≥κd\geq\sqrt{\kappa} imply ϱκ2​d≤e−2<1/3\varrho_{\kappa}^{2d}\leq e^{-2}<1/3. The formula for MM in the same lemma yields M≥d/(2​κ)≥d(1+δ)/2/2M\geq d/(2\sqrt{\kappa})\geq d^{(1+\delta)/2}/2. Together with the bound on τ\tau above, these estimates imply

τβ≤C′bd−δ/4(logd)3⟶0,Mβ2≥b22d⟶∞.\frac{\tau}{\beta}\leq\frac{C^{\prime}}{b}d^{-\delta/4}(\log d)^{3}\longrightarrow 0,\qquad M\beta^{2}\geq\frac{b^{2}}{2}\sqrt{d}\longrightarrow\infty.

All estimates are uniform over the stated parameter range. We may therefore choose d0​(δ)d_{0}(\delta) so that the conditions for the algorithmic bound above hold and, additionally, τ≤β/4\tau\leq\beta/4 and M​β2≥320M\beta^{2}\geq 320.

Now fix AA, draw Y∼πAY\sim\pi_{A}, and set Z=SA​(Y)Z=S_{A}(Y). Lemma 4.5 gives mean (−1)n​μn=β​M(-1)^{n}\mu_{n}=\beta M for the signed cosine quadratic form and mean MM for ‖Y‖2\|Y\|^{2}. Both variances are at most 2​M2M. Hence, using the L2L^{2} triangle inequality for centered variables,

𝔼​Z=(β−2​τ)​M≥β​M2,Var⁡(Z)≤(2​M+2​τ​2​M)2≤8​M.\mathbb{E}Z=(\beta-2\tau)M\geq\frac{\beta M}{2},\qquad\operatorname{Var}(Z)\leq\bigl(\sqrt{2M}+2\tau\sqrt{2M}\bigr)^{2}\leq 8M.

Chebyshev’s inequality gives, for every AA in the hard family,

πA​(EA)=ℙ⁡(Z>0)≥1−Var⁡(Z)(𝔼​Z)2≥1−32M​β2≥0.9.\pi_{A}(E_{A})=\mathbb{P}(Z>0)\geq 1-\frac{\operatorname{Var}(Z)}{(\mathbb{E}Z)^{2}}\geq 1-\frac{32}{M\beta^{2}}\geq 0.9.
Contradiction.

Finally, the per-input TV guarantee implies πA​(EA)−ρAAlg​(EA)≤ε\pi_{A}(E_{A})-\rho_{A}^{\mathrm{Alg}}(E_{A})\leq\varepsilon. Averaging over the random input and using the two probability bounds gives

0.89≤𝔼A​[πA​(EA)−ρAAlg​(EA)]≤ε≤0.1,0.89\leq\mathbb{E}_{A}\!\left[\pi_{A}(E_{A})-\rho_{A}^{\mathrm{Alg}}(E_{A})\right]\leq\varepsilon\leq 0.1,

a contradiction. ∎

4.4 Limitations of the Analysis

Theorem 4.1 is restricted to 2≤κ≤d1−δ2\leq\kappa\leq d^{1-\delta} for fixed δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1). Although it applies to every ε≤1/10\varepsilon\leq 1/10, its lower bound does not grow as ε\varepsilon decreases. We discuss two limitations of the analysis that affect extensions to larger condition numbers and higher accuracy.

Limitation on κ\kappa.

Our approach does not extend the Ω⁡(κ​log⁡d)\Omega(\sqrt{\kappa}\log d) lower bound to condition numbers κ≳d/log2⁡d\kappa\gtrsim d/\log^{2}d. Our proof controls the output of the algorithm by first applying Lemma 4.3 to place O⊤​XO^{\top}X in 𝒦q\mathcal{K}_{q}, and then bounding the cosine statistic uniformly over this space. However, the enlarged space 𝒦q\mathcal{K}_{q} has (q+1)2(q+1)^{2} generating vectors. Since the eigenvalues of Λ\Lambda are distinct, these vectors span a space of the following dimension.

Lemma 4.7 (Dimension of the Krylov space).

For every integer q≥0q\geq 0 and independent g1,…,gq+1∼N⁡(0,Id)g_{1},\ldots,g_{q+1}\allowbreak\sim N(0,I_{d}),

dim𝒦q=min⁡{d,(q+1)2}almost surely.\dim\mathcal{K}_{q}=\min\{d,(q+1)^{2}\}\qquad\text{almost surely}.

Once (q+1)2≥d(q+1)^{2}\geq d with q=Ω⁡(κ​log⁡d)q=\Omega(\sqrt{\kappa}\log d), we have 𝒦q=ℝd\mathcal{K}_{q}=\mathbb{R}^{d} almost surely. For n=2​q+1<dn=2q+1<d, the definition of θi\theta_{i} gives ∑idcos2⁡(n​θi)=d/2\sum_{i}^{d}\cos^{2}(n\theta_{i})=d/2, so at least one coordinate satisfies |cos⁡(n​θi)|≥1/2|\cos(n\theta_{i})|\geq 1/\sqrt{2}. Taking its coordinate unit vector yields

supu∈𝒦q∖{0}|u⊤​Dn​u|‖u‖2≥12.\sup_{u\in\mathcal{K}_{q}\setminus\{0\}}\frac{|u^{\top}D_{n}u|}{\|u\|^{2}}\geq\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.

Our separating test in Lemma 4.4 requires this supremum to be at most 1/21/2, which is incompatible with the displayed bound. Thus an argument based on a uniform bound over 𝒦q\mathcal{K}_{q} cannot apply once (q+1)2≥d(q+1)^{2}\geq d.

Limitation on accuracy.

Our test compares the ratio (−1)n​x⊤​O​Dn​O⊤​x/‖x‖2(-1)^{n}x^{\top}OD_{n}O^{\top}x/\|x\|^{2} with a threshold tt. Lemma 4.4 puts every output of the algorithm below tt only if t≥at\geq a, where aa is the uniform bound on 𝒦q\mathcal{K}_{q} that the lemma provides. Chebyshev’s inequality with Lemma 4.5 puts samples from the target above tt only if t<|μn|/Mt<|\mu_{n}|/M. Thus |μn|/M>a|\mu_{n}|/M>a, whatever the threshold. At the same time, the Bernstein calculation in the proof of Fact C.6 requires a≥c/da\geq c/\sqrt{d} even to certify a failure probability below one. Finally, Lemma 4.5 gives |μn|/M≤e−2n/κ|\mu_{n}|/M\leq e^{-2n/\sqrt{\kappa}}. Since n=2​q+1n=2q+1, we must have

cd≤a<|μn|M≤e−2(2q+1)/κ.\frac{c}{\sqrt{d}}\leq a<\frac{|\mu_{n}|}{M}\leq e^{-2(2q+1)/\sqrt{\kappa}}.

Taking logarithms yields q=O⁡(κ​log⁡d)q=O(\sqrt{\kappa}\log d), independently of ε\varepsilon. A different choice of the threshold or of the constants therefore cannot give a bound that grows as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0.

Remark 4.8 (Scope of the limitations).

These limitations concern our proof. We do not know whether the same fixed-spectrum family supports stronger lower bounds. Our analysis therefore leaves open whether the same fixed-spectrum family supports stronger lower bounds.

5 Conclusion

We proved an Ω⁡(min⁡{d,κ​log⁡(1+dκ​ε)})\Omega\bigl(\min\{d,\sqrt{\kappa}\log(1+\frac{d}{\sqrt{\kappa}\varepsilon})\}\bigr) query lower bound for Gaussian sampling. The bound comes from a construction with a hidden determinant sign and matches the known upper bound whenever κ≤d2−δ\kappa\leq d^{2-\delta} or ε≤d−c\varepsilon\leq d^{-c}, for fixed δ∈(0,2)\delta\in(0,2) and c>0c>0. We also extended the hidden-eigenbasis construction to growing condition numbers.

Closing the remaining gap for all condition numbers κ≤d2−δ\kappa\leq d^{2-\delta} at constant accuracy remains open. Our lower bounds also apply to strongly log-concave sampling, where the known upper bounds are much larger. It is open whether non-quadratic potentials are harder than Gaussians.

Appendix A Useful Facts

A.1 Two Spherical Poisson Identities

Both identities below are instances of the Poisson integral formula for the unit ball of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, applied at the point r​e1re_{1} to the harmonic functions 11 and y↦y1y\mapsto y_{1}.

Lemma A.1 (Spherical Poisson identities).

Let n≥2n\geq 2, and ζ=(ζ1,…,ζn)\zeta=(\zeta_{1},\dots,\zeta_{n}) be a uniform random point on 𝕊n−1\mathbb{S}^{n-1}, and let U=ζ1U=\zeta_{1} be its first coordinate., where n≥3n\geq 3. For every 0<r<10<r<1,

𝔼[(1+r2−2rU)−n/2]=11−r2,𝔼[U(1+r2−2rU)−n/2]=r1−r2.\mathbb{E}\left[(1+r^{2}-2rU)^{-n/2}\right]=\frac{1}{1-r^{2}},\qquad\mathbb{E}\left[U(1+r^{2}-2rU)^{-n/2}\right]=\frac{r}{1-r^{2}}. (12)
Proof.

Let σ\sigma be normalized surface measure on 𝕊n−1\mathbb{S}^{n-1}. By the Poisson representation formula [5, Theorem 1.21], every function hh harmonic on the unit ball and continuous on its closure satisfies

h⁡(a)=∫𝕊n−1h⁡(u)​1−‖a‖2‖u−a‖n​𝑑σ​(u),‖a‖<1.h(a)=\int_{\mathbb{S}^{n-1}}h(u)\frac{1-\|a\|^{2}}{\|u-a\|^{n}}\,d\sigma(u),\qquad\|a\|<1.

Apply this formula with a=r​e1a=re_{1} and, respectively, h⁡(x)=1h(x)=1 and h⁡(x)=x1h(x)=x_{1}. Since ‖u−r​e1‖2=1+r2−2​r​u1\|u-re_{1}\|^{2}=1+r^{2}-2ru_{1}, the two applications prove the lemma after division by 1−r21-r^{2}. ∎

B.2 Separation: Proof of Lemma 3.3

In this section, we prove Lemma 3.3.

Lemma B.5 (Separation (Lemma 6 restated)).

The averaged targets satisfy

The single-block argument combines a cancellation identity for Gaussian normalization factors with two spherical Poisson identities. Appendix C Proofs for Section 4

C.1 Proof of Lemma 4.3

To explain the argument, distinguish the original coordinates from the hidden eigenbasis: u=O⊤​xu=O^{\top}x expresses xx in the latter coordinates, where the matrix acts by u↦Λ​uu\mapsto\Lambda u. Thus a query at xix_{i} has hidden coordinates ui=O⊤​xiu_{i}=O^{\top}x_{i} and returns A​xi=O​Λ​uiAx_{i}=O\Lambda u_{i}. The algorithm observes xix_{i} and A​xiAx_{i} but the latent vector uiu_{i} is introduced for the analysis. The function value f⁡(xi)=⟨xi,A​xi⟩/2f(x_{i})=\langle x_{i},Ax_{i}\rangle/2 is determined by this pair and adds no information.

The difficulty is that xix_{i} may depend on earlier replies and hence on OO. We handle this dependence by revealing OO successively. Conditional on an enlarged history, OO is known on a revealed latent subspace and remains a Haar isometry between the complementary subspaces. Whenever the unrevealed component of O⊤​xiO^{\top}x_{i} is nonzero, its direction is uniform in the latent complement. We convert these directions into independent standard Gaussian vectors and propagate the resulting span relations under multiplication by Λ\Lambda. The extra vector gq+1g_{q+1} accounts for the output XX, which is treated as one final preimage revelation.

Throughout, for subspaces F,G⊆ℝdF,G\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} of equal dimension, we use the following notation:

  • •

    PFP_{F} is the orthogonal projection onto FF, 𝕊⁡(F)\mathbb{S}(F) is the unit sphere of FF, and Unif⁡(𝕊⁡(F))\operatorname{Unif}(\mathbb{S}(F)) is the uniform law on it.

  • •

    Iso⁡(F,G)\operatorname{Iso}(F,G) is the set of linear isometries from FF onto GG, and O⁡(F)=Iso⁡(F,F)\mathrm{O}(F)=\operatorname{Iso}(F,F). For J∈Iso⁡(F,G)J\in\operatorname{Iso}(F,G), J⊤:G→FJ^{\top}\colon G\to F denotes the adjoint, so J⊤=J−1J^{\top}=J^{-1}.

  • •

    Haar⁡(Iso⁡(F,G))\operatorname{Haar}(\operatorname{Iso}(F,G)) is the unique probability law on Iso⁡(F,G)\operatorname{Iso}(F,G) invariant under J↦U​J​Q⊤J\mapsto UJQ^{\top} for all U∈O⁡(G)U\in\mathrm{O}(G) and Q∈O⁡(F)Q\in\mathrm{O}(F). Equivalently, it is the law of U​J0UJ_{0} for U∼Haar⁡(O⁡(G))U\sim\operatorname{Haar}(\mathrm{O}(G)) and any fixed J0∈Iso⁡(F,G)J_{0}\in\operatorname{Iso}(F,G). If JJ has this law, then J−1J^{-1} has law Haar⁡(Iso⁡(G,F))\operatorname{Haar}(\operatorname{Iso}(G,F)).

  • •

    ℒ⁡(Y∣ℋ)\mathcal{L}(Y\mid\mathcal{H}) is the conditional law of a random element YY given a σ\sigma-algebra ℋ\mathcal{H}.

The key observation is that revealing one image–preimage pair of a Haar isometry preserves rotational symmetry on the orthogonal complements. Once J​v=wJv=w is known, orthogonal transformations fixing vv and ww preserve both this identity and the Haar law. Consequently, the remaining restriction is still a Haar isometry from F∩v⟂F\cap v^{\perp} onto G∩w⟂G\cap w^{\perp}. The following fact makes this observation precise, conditionally on the information already available.

Fact C.1 (Haar revelation).

Let F,GF,G be ℋ\mathcal{H}-measurable subspaces with dimF=dimG\dim F=\dim G, and let ℒ⁡(J∣ℋ)=Haar⁡(Iso⁡(F,G))\mathcal{L}(J\mid\mathcal{H})=\operatorname{Haar}(\operatorname{Iso}(F,G)). For an ℋ\mathcal{H}-measurable w∈𝕊⁡(G)w\in\mathbb{S}(G), put v=J⊤​wv=J^{\top}w. Then

ℒ⁡(v∣ℋ)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(v\mid\mathcal{H}) =Unif⁡(𝕊⁡(F)),\displaystyle=\operatorname{Unif}(\mathbb{S}(F)),
ℒ⁡(J|F∩v⟂∣ℋ,v)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(J|_{F\cap v^{\perp}}\mid\mathcal{H},v) =Haar⁡(Iso⁡(F∩v⟂,G∩w⟂)).\displaystyle=\operatorname{Haar}\bigl(\operatorname{Iso}(F\cap v^{\perp},G\cap w^{\perp})\bigr).

Symmetrically, for an ℋ\mathcal{H}-measurable s∈𝕊⁡(F)s\in\mathbb{S}(F) and t=J​st=Js, the vector tt is uniform on 𝕊⁡(G)\mathbb{S}(G) and, given (ℋ,t)(\mathcal{H},t), J|F∩s⟂J|_{F\cap s^{\perp}} is Haar on Iso⁡(F∩s⟂,G∩t⟂)\operatorname{Iso}(F\cap s^{\perp},G\cap t^{\perp}).

Proof.

Condition on ℋ\mathcal{H}. For any Q∈O⁡(F)Q\in\mathrm{O}(F), invariance gives J​Q⊤=dJJQ^{\top}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{d}}}{{=}}J, hence Q​v=dvQv\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{d}}}{{=}}v, so vv is uniform on 𝕊⁡(F)\mathbb{S}(F).

Next, let UU be Haar on the stabilizer {U∈O⁡(G):U​w=w}≅O⁡(G∩w⟂)\{U\in\mathrm{O}(G):Uw=w\}\cong\mathrm{O}(G\cap w^{\perp}), independent of JJ, and set J′=U​JJ^{\prime}=UJ. Then J′=dJJ^{\prime}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{d}}}{{=}}J and J′⁣⊤​w=J⊤​U⊤​w=vJ^{\prime\top}w=J^{\top}U^{\top}w=v, so (J′,v)=d(J,v)(J^{\prime},v)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{d}}}{{=}}(J,v). The symmetric statement follows by applying the above to J⊤=J−1J^{\top}=J^{-1}, which is Haar on Iso⁡(G,F)\operatorname{Iso}(G,F). ∎

Haar states.

To apply Fact C.1 repeatedly along an adaptive transcript, we need to keep track of which part of OO has been revealed and how the remaining part is distributed. We record the available information by a σ\sigma-algebra ℋ\mathcal{H} and the revealed directions in the hidden eigenbasis by a subspace EE. The history should determine both EE and the action of OO on EE, represented by O​PEOP_{E}, while the restriction of OO to E⟂E^{\perp} should remain Haar between the corresponding orthogonal complements. The following definition packages these requirements into a state that we will preserve after each revelation.

Definition C.2 (Haar state).

Let ℋ\mathcal{H} be a σ\sigma-algebra and E⊆ℝdE\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} a random subspace. We call (ℋ,E)(\mathcal{H},E) a Haar state if EE and O​PEOP_{E} are ℋ\mathcal{H}-measurable and

ℒ⁡(O|E⟂∣ℋ)=Haar⁡(Iso⁡(E⟂,(O​E)⟂)).\mathcal{L}(O|_{E^{\perp}}\mid\mathcal{H})=\operatorname{Haar}\bigl(\operatorname{Iso}(E^{\perp},(OE)^{\perp})\bigr).

We next show that the Haar-state property is preserved by the revelations needed to process an oracle query. For a query point xx chosen using the current history, we first reveal its hidden coordinates u=O⊤​xu=O^{\top}x, and then reveal the reply A​x=O​Λ​uAx=O\Lambda u. These two steps add uu and Λ​u\Lambda u, respectively, to the revealed latent subspace. We will also introduce independent auxiliary randomness for the Gaussian construction below. The following fact verifies that all three updates preserve a Haar state and identifies the uniform direction arising from a preimage revelation.
